questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Dimensions of Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $6?$

- ${R}_{5}[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $5$
- ${R}^{5}$
- ${\text{M}}_{6}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 6$ matrices over $R$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

- Recall that $\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{5}[t])=5+1=6.\,✓
$$
- Recall that $\text{dim}({R}^{n})=n.$ Therefore, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{5})=5\ne 6.\,\times 
$$
- Recall that $\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n}(R))={n}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6}(R))={6}^{2}=36\ne 6.\,\times 
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Dimension of a Matrix Vector Space Given Its Standard Basis
questions.problem: What is the dimension of ${\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R),$ the vector space of all $6\times 4$ matrices over $R?$
questions.worked_solution:
The standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R)$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of ${\text{M}}_{3\times 2}(R)$ contains $3\cdot 2=6$ elements, and is given by

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Therefore, for ${\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R),$ we have

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{6\times 4}(R))=6\cdot 4=24.
$$

In general, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{n\times m}(R))=n\cdot m.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Finite and Infinite-Dimensional Vector Spaces
questions.problem:
Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

- $D(R),$ the vector space of all differentiable functions on $R$
- ${\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R),$ the vector space of all $10\times 100$ matrices over $R$
- ${R}_{200}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $200$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $D(R)$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of $D(R)$ is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $D(R)$  of size $n,$ which imples that $D(R)$ cannot have finite dimension.     .

- ${\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R)$ and ${R}_{200}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R))=10\cdot 100=1\,000
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{200}[t])=200+1=201,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

- $D(R),$ the vector space of all differentiable functions on $R$
- ${R}^{100}$
- ${R}_{2000}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2\,000$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $D(R)$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of $D(R)$ is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $D(R)$  of size $n,$ which imples that $D(R)$ cannot have finite dimension.     .

- ${R}^{100}$ and ${R}_{2000}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{100})=100
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{2000}[t])=2000+1=2\,001,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
